THE FACTS

I.  THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

14.  The applicant was born in 1973 and has lived in Vienna since 1999, when she left Istanbul to pursue her medical studies at the Faculty of Medicine at Vienna University.

facts.text: The applicant comes from a traditional family of practising Muslims and considers it her religious duty to wear the Islamic headscarf.

anchor.surface_text: ...She comes from a traditional family of practising Muslims and considers it her religious duty to wear the Islamic headscarf.

facts.text: On 26 August 1997 the applicant, then in her fifth year at the Faculty of Medicine at Bursa University, enrolled at the Cerrahpaşa Faculty of Medicine at Istanbul University.

anchor.surface_text:
A.  The circular of 23 February 1998

15.  On 26 August 1997 the applicant, then in her fifth year at the Faculty of Medicine at Bursa University, enrolled at the Cerrahpaşa Faculty of Medicine at Istanbul University.

facts.text: The applicant wore the Islamic headscarf during the four years she studied medicine at Bursa University and continued to do so until February 1998.

anchor.surface_text: She says she wore the Islamic headscarf during the four years she spent studying medicine at the University of Bursa and continued to do so until February 1998.

facts.text: On 23 February 1998 the Vice-Chancellor of Istanbul University issued a circular prohibiting students wearing the Islamic headscarf or with beards from attending lectures, courses or tutorials.

anchor.surface_text:
16.  On 23 February 1998 the Vice-Chancellor of Istanbul University issued a circular, the relevant part of which provides:

“By virtue of the Constitution, the law and regulations, and in accordance with the case-law of the Supreme Administrative Court and the European Commission of Human Rights and the resolutions adopted by the university administrative boards, students whose ‘heads are covered’ (who wear the Islamic headscarf) and students (including overseas students) with beards must not be admitted to lectures, courses or tutorials.

facts.text: On 12 March 1998 the applicant was denied access to a written examination on oncology because she was wearing the Islamic headscarf.

anchor.surface_text: On 12 March 1998, in accordance with the aforementioned circular, the applicant was denied access by invigilators to a written examination on oncology because she was wearing the Islamic headscarf.

facts.text: On 20 March 1998 the secretariat of the chair of orthopaedic traumatology refused to allow the applicant to enrol because she was wearing a headscarf.

anchor.surface_text: On 20 March 1998 the secretariat of the chair of orthopaedic traumatology refused to allow her to enrol because she was wearing a headscarf.

facts.text: On 16 April 1998 the applicant was refused admission to a neurology lecture because she was wearing the Islamic headscarf.

anchor.surface_text: On 16 April 1998 she was refused admission to a neurology lecture and on 10 June 1998 to a written examination on public health, again for the same reason.

facts.text: On 10 June 1998 the applicant was refused admission to a written examination on public health because she was wearing the Islamic headscarf.

anchor.surface_text: ...and on 10 June 1998 to a written examination on public health, again for the same reason.

facts.text: On 29 July 1998 the applicant lodged an application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998, alleging it infringed her rights under Articles 8, 9, 14 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text:
B.  The application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998

18.  On 29 July 1998 the applicant lodged an application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998. In her written pleadings, she submitted that the circular and its implementation had infringed her rights guaranteed by Articles 8, 9 and 14 of the Convention and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, in that there was no statutory basis for the circular and the Vice-Chancellor’s Office had no regulatory power in that sphere.

facts.text: On 19 March 1999 the Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's application, holding the Vice-Chancellor had power to regulate students' dress under section 13(b) of the Higher Education Act.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  In a judgment of 19 March 1999, the Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the application, holding that by virtue of section 13(b) of the Higher Education Act (Law no. 2547 – see paragraph 52 below) a university vice-chancellor, as the executive organ of the university, had power to regulate students’ dress for the purposes of maintaining order.

facts.text: On 19 April 2001 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed an appeal on points of law by the applicant against the dismissal of her application.

anchor.surface_text: 20.  On 19 April 2001 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed an appeal on points of law by the applicant.

facts.text: In May 1998 disciplinary proceedings were brought against the applicant for failing to comply with the rules on dress.

anchor.surface_text:
C.  The disciplinary measures taken against the applicant

21.  In May 1998 disciplinary proceedings were brought against the applicant under paragraph 6 (a) of the Students Disciplinary Procedure Rules (see paragraph 50 below) as a result of her failure to comply with the rules on dress.

facts.text: On 26 May 1998 the dean of the faculty issued the applicant a warning for her attitude and failure to comply with the rules on dress.

anchor.surface_text: 22.  On 26 May 1998, in view of the fact that the applicant had shown by her actions that she intended to continue wearing the headscarf to lectures and/or tutorials, the dean of the faculty declared that her attitude and failure to comply with the rules on dress were not befitting of a student. He therefore decided to issue her with a warning.

facts.text: On 15 February 1999 an unauthorised assembly gathered outside the deanery of the Cerrahpaşa Faculty of Medicine to protest against the rules on dress.

anchor.surface_text: 23.  On 15 February 1999 an unauthorised assembly gathered outside the deanery of the Cerrahpaşa Faculty of Medicine to protest against the rules on dress.

facts.text: On 26 February 1999 the dean began disciplinary proceedings against various students, including the applicant, for joining the assembly.

anchor.surface_text: 24.  On 26 February 1999 the dean of the faculty began disciplinary proceedings against various students, including the applicant, for joining the assembly.

facts.text: On 13 April 1999, after hearing her representations, the dean suspended the applicant from the university for a semester.

anchor.surface_text: On 13 April 1999, after hearing her representations, he suspended her from the university for a semester pursuant to Article 9 (j) of the Students Disciplinary Procedure Rules (see paragraph 50 below).

facts.text: On 10 June 1999 the applicant lodged an application with the Istanbul Administrative Court for an order quashing the suspension decision.

anchor.surface_text: 25.  On 10 June 1999 the applicant lodged an application with the Istanbul Administrative Court for an order quashing the decision to suspend her.

facts.text: On 30 November 1999 the Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the application, holding the suspension was not illegal.

anchor.surface_text: The application was dismissed on 30 November 1999 by the Istanbul Administrative Court on the ground that, in the light of the material in the case file and the settled case-law on the subject, the impugned measure could not be regarded as illegal.

facts.text: On 28 June 2000 Law no. 4584 entered into force, providing amnesty for students for disciplinary penalties and annulling any resulting disability.

anchor.surface_text: 26.  Following the entry into force of Law no. 4584 on 28 June 2000 (which provided for students to be given an amnesty in respect of penalties imposed for disciplinary offences and for any resulting disability to be annulled), the applicant was granted an amnesty releasing her from all the penalties that had been imposed on her and the resultant disabilities.

facts.text: On 28 September 2000 the Supreme Administrative Court held that Law no. 4584 made it unnecessary to examine the merits of the applicant’s appeal against the judgment of 30 November 1999.

anchor.surface_text: 27.  On 28 September 2000 the Supreme Administrative Court held that Law no. 4584 made it unnecessary to examine the merits of the applicant’s appeal on points of law against the judgment of 30 November 1999.

facts.text: On 16 September 1999 the applicant abandoned her studies in Turkey and enrolled at Vienna University to pursue her university education.

anchor.surface_text: 28.  In the meantime, on 16 September 1999, the applicant abandoned her studies in Turkey and enrolled at Vienna University, where she pursued her university education.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that there was no statutory basis for the circular and that the Vice-Chancellor’s Office had no regulatory power to prohibit wearing the headscarf.

anchor.surface_text: In her written pleadings, she submitted that the circular and its implementation had infringed her rights guaranteed by Articles 8, 9 and 14 of the Convention and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, in that there was no statutory basis for the circular and the Vice-Chancellor’s Office had no regulatory power in that sphere.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the circular was issued within the statutory framework and based on settled case-law, thus having a legal basis.

arguments.claim: The applicant contended that the interference was not foreseeable and was not based on a law within the meaning of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant considered that the interference with her right had not been foreseeable and was not based on a “law” within the meaning of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the law was accessible and sufficiently precise to satisfy foreseeability requirements.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that the legislature had not introduced legislation prohibiting the Islamic headscarf and that the courts only apply law, not establish new legal rules.

anchor.surface_text: She explained that under the Students Disciplinary Procedure Rules it was not a disciplinary offence merely to wear the Islamic headscarf (see paragraphs 49 and 50 above). The first regulation to restrict her right to wear the headscarf had been the circular issued by the Vice-Chancellor on 23 February 1998, some four and a half years later.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted that the circular was issued within the statutory framework and based on settled case-law, which includes judge-made law as part of the legal basis.

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that the Vice-Chancellor had no authority under law or disciplinary rules to refuse access to students wearing the headscarf.

anchor.surface_text: In the instant case, the Vice-Chancellor had not possessed the authority or power, either under the laws in force or the Students Disciplinary Procedure Rules, to refuse students “wearing the headscarf” access to university premises or examination rooms.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the Vice-Chancellor acted within powers delegated by law and consistent with case-law.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that the legislature had never supported a general ban on wearing religious signs in schools and universities.

anchor.surface_text: Moreover, the fact that the administrative authorities had not introduced any general regulations providing for the imposition of disciplinary penalties on students wearing the headscarf in institutions of higher education meant that no such ban existed.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court stated it is not its role to assess legislative methods but to determine conformity with the Convention, and found the legal basis sufficient.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that students were adults capable of deciding what was appropriate conduct and that wearing the headscarf did not restrict others' freedoms or show disrespect.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant further explained in her aforementioned observations that students were discerning adults who enjoyed full legal capacity and were capable of deciding for themselves what was appropriate conduct. Consequently, the allegation that, by wearing the Islamic headscarf, she had shown a lack of respect for the convictions of others or sought to influence fellow students and to undermine their rights and freedoms was wholly unfounded.
